taste.summary: Left to ripen to golden-green on the tree it is crisp, juicy and richly sweet, with a honeyed, pear-drop note and only modest acidity; a few tasters also pick up a faint ginger or cinnamon warmth. Fruit picked green and held in long storage is the bland, soft, crumbly supermarket apple. Holds its shape when cooked.

Firm, crisp, juicy cream flesh; sharp, with a slightly astringent, distinctly cider-like back-taste, though tasters find enough sweetness to eat it fresh straight from the tree. Cooks down to a well-flavoured purée; it is not a keeper and is best used early.

Firm, fine white flesh, juicy and sharply acid, though fully ripe fruit is almost sweet enough to eat raw. In the pan it collapses quickly into a pale, creamy, tart purée with a fine, heady apple scent, ideal for sauce and early-season pies; it keeps only a week or so.

Firm, crisp, fine-grained yellow-white flesh with a rich, sweet and noticeably spicy flavour, fuller than its offspring Golden Delicious, with a clean, dry finish; one taster also notes a slight pear flavour. Keeps into February; good fresh and in pies, sauce, apple butter and cider.

Very firm, crisp, juicy red flesh with a bright sweet-tart balance and fruity berry and citrus notes; quite sharp if picked early, sweeter after a few weeks, and it can last into February. Flavour depends on site: one grower found it never developed real flavour at a research station.

Juicy, fairly soft yet dense yellowish flesh, sweet with a richly spiced acidity when fully ripe and an aromatic, Cox-like character; several tasters note a pineapple flavour. Prized for its orange-tinted juice; keeps only a month or two and is best eaten cool.

Famous for its texture: large cells that fracture with a light, juicy crunch rather than a hard, dense one. Flavour is mainly sweet with little acidity or depth, sometimes with a faint pear-drop or honeyed note; a well-grown fruit is refreshing, an ordinary one simply sweet. Stays crisp in store until spring, and the flavour can improve for a week or so after leaving cold storage.

Tender, juicy, yellowish-white flesh with a fresh sweet-tart balance; Scandinavian sources praise its pleasant aroma and one taster finds a hint of Cox, but Orange Pippin rates the flavour light and rather bland. Best soon after picking, though it can be stored into the new year; a traditional Christmas apple in Scandinavia.

White, very juicy flesh that is soft rather than crisp, with a lively, rather sharp flavour and a distinct peach-like aroma that gives the variety its name. It does not keep: eat within days of picking.

A very hard, dense, crunchy apple with juicy butter-yellow flesh and a strong sweet-sharp flavour led by a pronounced pear-drop note; tasters also report floral, honeyed and occasionally banana or clove hints. Well-coloured fruit tastes best - poorly coloured apples are flatter and closer to Braeburn - and the firmness holds for months in store.

Crisp, juicy, creamy-white flesh with a honeyed sweetness from Golden Delicious, kept lively by plenty of balancing acidity from Jonathan; some tasters note a subtle pear-drop sweetness. Best within a month or two of picking: it softens quickly out of the fridge and turns greasy in long storage, so supermarket fruit is often disappointing.

A strong, very fruity Cox-type apple, sweet but noticeably sharper than its parent, with an intense, well-balanced flavour some tasters compare to Topaz. Juicy cream flesh with a green tinge, dense and firm rather than crunchy; it keeps a month or two before softening.

Firm, fairly crisp and very juicy, with a mild, clean flavour that leans sharp rather than sweet and a light, vinous aftertaste. More delicate and less pronounced than its sibling Jazz; some tasters find a nectarine-like fruitiness, others want more sweetness.

Very juicy, pale cream flesh on the softer side of crunchy, with a mild apple flavour, a refreshing touch of acidity and, in a good year, a hint of strawberry inherited from Worcester Pearmain. Pleasant rather than deep; it softens within a week or so (keep it chilled) and gives an attractive pink-orange juice.
